items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n] is a random sample of size [MATH: n] from a distribution with population mean [MATH: \mu] and population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] Let's define a new random variable as the sum of all [MATH: X_i]'s as follows:

Content:
[MATH: X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i]

Content:
The sample mean [MATH: \overline{X}] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \overline{X} = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i]
which is equivalent to
[MATH: n\cdot \overline{X} =\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.]

Content:
Therefore, our random variable [MATH: X] is simply the product of [MATH: n] with the sample mean:
[MATH: X = n\cdot \overline{X}.]

Content:
Now, the central limit theorem (CLT) states that for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] the distribution of [MATH: \overline{X}] can be approximated as
[MATH: \overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).]

Content:
Therefore, since
[MATH: \textrm{E}[\overline X] = \mu, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\overline X] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}]

Content:
we can calculate [MATH: \textrm E[X]] and [MATH: \textrm{Var}[X]] using the properties of mean and variance as follows:

Content:
[MATH: E[X]|= E[nX^(―)]; = n ⋅ E[X^(―)]; = nμ; Var[X]|= Var[nX^(―)]; = n^{2} ⋅ Var[X^(―)]; = n^{2} ⋅ (σ^{2})/(n); = nσ^{2}]

Content:
Finally, since [MATH: \overline{X}] is (approximately) normally distributed, we have that [MATH: X] is also approximately normal. Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: X\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2).]

Content:
This is an important result. It tells us that provided that we have a sufficiently large I.I.D. sample, the sum of the elements from that sample is approximately normally distributed with mean [MATH: n\mu] and variance [MATH: n\sigma^2.] This result does not depend on the distribution of the [MATH: X_i]'s!

Let [MATH: X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_{110} \sim U[1,5]] be an I.I.D. sample of size [MATH: 110] from the continuous uniform distribution on the interval [MATH: [1,5].] Suppose we define the random variable [MATH: X] as [MATH: X = \sum_{i=1}^{110} X_i.]

What is the approximate distribution of [MATH: X?]
sections.readable_text:
Let [MATH: X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_{110} \sim U[1,5]] be an I.I.D. sample of size [MATH: 110] from the continuous uniform distribution on the interval [MATH: [1,5].] Suppose we define the random variable [MATH: X] as
[MATH: X = \sum_{i=1}^{110} X_i.]

What is the approximate distribution of [MATH: X?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the central limit theorem states the following:

Suppose that [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n] is a random sample of size [MATH: n] from a population with a population mean [MATH: \mu] and population standard deviation [MATH: \sigma.] The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] the distribution of the sample mean [MATH: \overline{X}] can be approximated as [MATH: \overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).]

Moreover, if we define

[MATH: X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i]

then, by the properties of mean and variance, we have

[MATH: \textrm{E}[X] = n\mu, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = n\sigma^2]

and consequently,

[MATH: X\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2).]

The expected value and the variance of a uniform random variable [MATH: X_i \sim U[a,b]] can be found as

[MATH: \textrm{E}[X_i] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X_i] = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{12}.]

So, in our case, we have

[MATH: n|= 110,; μ|= E[X_{i}]; = (a + b)/(2); = (1 + 5)/(2); = (6)/(2); = 3,; σ^{2}|= Var[X_{i}]; = ((b − a)^{2})/(12); = ((5 − 1)^{2})/(12); = (16)/(12); = (4)/(3).]

Therefore, for the approximate distribution of [MATH: X,] we obtain

[MATH: X|∼N(nμ, nσ^{2}); ∼N(110 ⋅ 3, 110 ⋅ (4)/(3)); ∼N(330, (440)/(3)).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

Suppose that [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n] is a random sample of size [MATH: n] from a population with a population mean [MATH: \mu] and population standard deviation [MATH: \sigma.] The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] the distribution of the sample mean [MATH: \overline{X}] can be approximated as [MATH: \overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).]

The expected value and the variance of a binomial random variable [MATH: X_i \sim B(m,p)] can be found as

[MATH: \textrm{E}[X_i] = mp, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X_i] = mp(1-p).]

So, in our case, we have [MATH: n|= 66,; μ|= E[X_{i}]; = mp; = 25 ⋅ (9)/(20); = (45)/(4),; σ^{2}|= Var[X_{i}]; = mp(1 − p); = 25 ⋅ (9)/(20) ⋅ (11)/(20); = (99)/(16).]

Therefore, for the approximate distribution of the sample mean [MATH: \overline{X},] we obtain [MATH: X^(―)|∼N(μ, (σ^{2})/(n)); ∼N((45)/(4), (99)/(16) ⋅ (1)/(66)); ∼N((45)/(4), (3)/(32)).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the central limit theorem states the following:

Suppose that [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n] is a random sample of size [MATH: n] from a population with a population mean [MATH: \mu] and population standard deviation [MATH: \sigma.] The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] the distribution of the sample mean [MATH: \overline{X}] can be approximated as [MATH: \overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).]

Moreover, if we define

[MATH: X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i]

then by the properties of mean and variance, we have

[MATH: \textrm{E}[X] = n\mu, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = n\sigma^2]

and consequently,

[MATH: X\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2).]

The expected value and the variance of a geometric random variable [MATH: X_i \sim \textrm{Geom}(p)] can be found as

[MATH: \textrm{E}[X_i] = \dfrac{1}{p}, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X_i] = \dfrac{1-p}{p^2}.]

So, in our case, we have

[MATH: n|= 80,; μ|= E[X_{i}]; = (1)/(p); = (1)/(0.4); = (5)/(2),; σ^{2}|= Var[X_{i}]; = (1 − p)/(p^{2}); = (1 − 0.4)/(0.4^{2}); = (0.6)/(0.16); = (15)/(4).]

Therefore, for the approximate distribution of [MATH: X,] we obtain

[MATH: X|∼N(nμ, nσ^{2}); ∼N(80 ⋅ (5)/(2), 80 ⋅ (15)/(4)); ∼N(200, 300).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n] is a random sample of size [MATH: n] from a distribution with population mean [MATH: \mu] and population variance [MATH: \sigma^2.] Let's define a new random variable as the sum of all [MATH: X_i]'s as follows:

Content:
[MATH: X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i]

Content:
The sample mean [MATH: \overline{X}] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \overline{X} = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i]
which is equivalent to
[MATH: n\cdot \overline{X} =\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.]

Content:
Therefore, our random variable [MATH: X] is simply the product of [MATH: n] with the sample mean:
[MATH: X = n\cdot \overline{X}.]

Content:
Now, the central limit theorem (CLT) states that for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] the distribution of [MATH: \overline{X}] can be approximated as
[MATH: \overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).]

Content:
Therefore, since
[MATH: \textrm{E}[\overline X] = \mu, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\overline X] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}]

Content:
we can calculate [MATH: \textrm E[X]] and [MATH: \textrm{Var}[X]] using the properties of mean and variance as follows:

Content:
[MATH: E[X]|= E[nX^(―)]; = n ⋅ E[X^(―)]; = nμ; Var[X]|= Var[nX^(―)]; = n^{2} ⋅ Var[X^(―)]; = n^{2} ⋅ (σ^{2})/(n); = nσ^{2}]

Content:
Finally, since [MATH: \overline{X}] is (approximately) normally distributed, we have that [MATH: X] is also approximately normal. Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: X\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2).]

Content:
This is an important result. It tells us that provided that we have a sufficiently large I.I.D. sample, the sum of the elements from that sample is approximately normally distributed with mean [MATH: n\mu] and variance [MATH: n\sigma^2.] This result does not depend on the distribution of the [MATH: X_i]'s!

---

Item 2 — Example: Applying the CLT to Continuous Uniform Random Variables

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_{110} \sim U[1,5]] be an I.I.D. sample of size [MATH: 110] from the continuous uniform distribution on the interval [MATH: [1,5].] Suppose we define the random variable [MATH: X] as
[MATH: X = \sum_{i=1}^{110} X_i.]

What is the approximate distribution of [MATH: X?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the central limit theorem states the following:

> Suppose that [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n] is a random sample of size [MATH: n] from a population with a population mean [MATH: \mu] and population standard deviation [MATH: \sigma.] The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] the distribution of the sample mean [MATH: \overline{X}] can be approximated as
> [MATH: \overline{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).]

Moreover, if we define

[MATH: X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i]

then, by the properties of mean and variance, we have

[MATH: \textrm{E}[X] = n\mu, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = n\sigma^2]

and consequently,

[MATH: X\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2).]

The expected value and the variance of a uniform random variable [MATH: X_i \sim U[a,b]] can be found as

[MATH: \textrm{E}[X_i] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}, \qquad
\textrm{Var}[X_i] = \dfrac{(b-a)^2}{12}.]

So, in our case, we have

[MATH: n|= 110,; μ|= E[X_{i}]; = (a + b)/(2); = (1 + 5)/(2); = (6)/(2); = 3,; σ^{2}|= Var[X_{i}]; = ((b − a)^{2})/(12); = ((5 − 1)^{2})/(12); = (16)/(12); = (4)/(3).]

Therefore, for the approximate distribution of [MATH: X,] we obtain

[MATH: X|∼N(nμ, nσ^{2}); ∼N(110 ⋅ 3, 110 ⋅ (4)/(3)); ∼N(330, (440)/(3)).]
